newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW - Canada Feb unemployment rate flat.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Canada Feb unemployment rate flat.

text.p: Following are reactions to unemployment data released by Statistics Canada on Friday. Statistics Canada said on Friday the unemployment rate was unchanged at 9.7 in February from January. Employment fell by 18,700 to 13.7 million.
Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast, on average, that the rate would drop to 9.6 percent.
David Rosenberg, senior economist, Nesbitt Burns Inc -- "It was an absolutely stunningly soft report with no redeeming features.

Rosenberg -- "It's not a pretty picture for the economy and not a pretty picture for the Canadian dollar...Headline figures like these are going to keep the Bank of Canada holding fast for a while and with (Federal Reserve Chairman) Mr. (Alan) Greenspan set to pull the trigger soon, I would suggest long the Canadian dollar is not where you want to be."

Randall Powley, senior economist, ScotiaMcLeod - "These numbers to me don't make any sense at all. I think that this is a reflection of the new (redesigned employment) survey that's been brought in over the last five months.

Powley - "There are certain parts of it that make sense. The 27,000 loss in retail isn't out of the ballpark given that we had a big run-up in the fourth quarter and now we are in a slower sales season...The agricultural part makes some sense because (agricultural) prices are down fairly substantially.

"But the rest of it just isn't in line with the strength we are seeing in the rest of the economy...In the fourth quarter last year, we saw very little growth in employment and we saw a 6.8 percent annualized increase in labor income. Now unless someone's getting some massive wage increases, there had to be some jobs out there."
Avery Shenfeld, senior economist, CIBC Wood Gundy Inc - "It's another blow to those who were suggesting the Canadian economy was on the verge of a real take-off.

"Some of the jobs we may never have had -- we lost a lot of jobs in agriculture that looked like a statistical fluke when we gained them late last year. But this only increases the length of the road ahead of us before we can get interest rates working their magic.
"I think this underscores the fact that the Bank of Canada will not be eager to match the Federal Reserve on rate hikes this year."
